Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas: one focuses on using unlimited training images, often employing an unconstrained field of view, and the other deals with limited-data pose estimation. For the latter, DoF estimation can be challenging due to a crowded background and limited training images. In this work, we introduce an end-to-end network, named DeepHMap++, to estimate the 6D pose of objects in low-training-image scenarios. DeepHMap++ builds upon our prior work, integrating projection grouping and correspondence learning. Specifically, it generates a binary mask to remove distracting background, a feature map to reduce clutter, and a fully connected network to establish correspondences between a 2D image and a rendered template. We also introduce a novel orientation regression module to predict the object's rotational pose. DeepHMap++ was used to train a network for estimating the pose of a VGG Block, and also another for estimating the pose of a soccer, however, our primary experiment utilizes VGG Block as the object of interest. Experimentation shows that our network surpasses current state-of-the-art performance on the LVIS dataset by a significant margin. Furthermore, the efficacy of our approach is demonstrated by conducting multiple ablation studies. In addition, we found that training the network on easy poses resulted in improved performance, also discovered the effectiveness of our orientation regression module as well as the validity of our approach for positive hard mining. In total, we discovered 12 possible easy poses out of 50 possible poses and achieved a 6D pose estimation accuracy of 85% on the LVIS dataset. In conclusion, we presented DeepHMap++: a robust network for estimating the 6D pose of objects in low-training-image scenarios, also demonstrated its capability for training on easy poses. The code has been made publicly available at: https://github.com/ghaith/DeepHMap++-pose-estimation.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than at low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity, and secondary-closure pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. Our research involved both high-speed visualization of low-density spheres entering water and analysis of existing data for higher-density spheres. Our results provide a framework for further studies on this complex, intermediate-speed water-entry regime. Our findings are relevant to a wide range of situations involving impact with water's surface, including accidents, operations, and equipment design. Our discovery of the significance of pressures within the formed cavity during the water-entry interaction, known as surface seal, also has implications for the more general phenomenon of cavity formation in water. Our research involved both a steel sphere entering water at mid-range speeds and a comprehensive review of existing research, with results from our experiments and data analysis presented in the form of images, along with graphs and tables of measurements and derived values. Our study provides a foundation for further investigations, including ones on the pressures within the formed cavity, the pressures exerted on the sphere as it enters the water, and the water-entry interactions at mid-range speeds with different water depths and different shapes of spheres. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching, and post-selection cat states, and how they are influenced by the catalytic device used. Our findings also highlight the distinct ways in which these states behave when interacting with a photon detector or a cavity system. We discuss the importance of SPCCSs in quantum communication, and examine the potential of post-selection cat states to facilitate the transmission of classical information over a quantum channel. Lastly, we outline the experimental requirements necessary to generate SPCCSs, and discuss the limitations associated with detecting these states, as well as the impact of lossy environments on their formation. Our work demonstrates that SPCCSs generated via quantum-optical catalysis possess unique quantum properties, as well as distinct phase space structures, as seen in the variations of their Wigner functions. We propose that these states could be utilized for developing a precise quantum error correction protocol known as quantum classical-quantum classical, as well as for generating non-classical correlations in open quantum systems. We also outline the possibilities for experimentally producing SPCCSs using available resources, as well as the potential to generate cat states and close the quantum classical gap. We believe that investigating these states will facilitate significant breakthroughs in quantum information processing, as well as provide valuable insights into the behavior of non-equilibrium open quantum systems. We propose that the term single-photon catalyzed coherent states be abbreviated as SPCCS. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring these additional data sources is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we aim to develop a more independent method for detecting esophageal tumors by solely using CT scans without complementary information. We have created a novel neural network called DDAUnet that consists of a dense attention module and a dense residual module to enhance the performance of dense networks. We have also introduced a new technique called dilated dense attention to improve performance. In experiments using publicly available datasets, our model showed superior results to existing models, and further analysis revealed the importance of dense networks, the effectiveness of the proposed technique, and the limited value of complementary information in this specific case. This could be verified by training the model using complementary information and comparing the outcomes to a model trained without this information. This finding has significant implications for reducing medical costs and making more effective use of limited resources. This achievement has also been demonstrated on a related task called airway segmentation in head CT scans. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles' potential medical applications. However, theoretical studies of these materials are hindered by uncertainty about their fundamental structure. There are three competing structures being considered: a disordered form known as $\alpha$-Ta$_2$O$_5$, two ordered forms known as $\beta$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ and $\gamma$-Ta$_2$ O$_5$, with the latter being particularly challenging to study due to its high energy requirements. By using a combination of Monte Carlo methods and first-principles simulations, we have investigated Ta$_2$O$_5$'s ground state configuration and potential pathways for $\alpha$ to $\beta$ or $\gamma$ transition. Monte Carlo simulations facilitated access to $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ through high temperature and pressure conditions, but revealed that this state of matter is unstable at lower temperatures, existing instead as a $\beta$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure with a particular rotation angle. This angle can be associated with an energy barrier that $\alpha$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ lacks, implying that $\alpha$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ is its ground state. This finding is also consistent with experimental results showing that at lower temperatures Ta$_2$O$_5$ lacks disorder. This could be achieved by subjecting Ta$_2$O$_5$ to lower temperatures and pressures than previously thought, and also through another pathway that involves a more complex sequence of transformations. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of Reddit, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. In such areas, initiatives aimed at reducing misinformation may need to address underlying societal issues rather than solely focusing on digital solutions. In regions with more resilient communities, we suggested targeted interventions that promote social cohesion and encourage better information literacy. In areas characterized by opportunistic personalities, we found increased circulation of news related to sports and entertainment, and recommended tailored approaches that take into account the specific demands of these communities. In addition to these findings, we discovered that misinformation dissemination varied significantly across states, with North and South Dakota leading the pack, followed by Montana, Alaska, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Arkansas, Kansas, Iowa, Minnesota, and Wyoming. In contrast, cities with high population densities, such as Santa Clara, San Francisco, Alameda, New York, Kings, and Queens counties, exhibited lower levels of misinformation dissemination. We concluded that The Big Sort plays a crucial role in the spread of online misinformation and that policymakers and platform leaders may need to consider its implications in order to effectively mitigate the problem. We also outlined potential research paths in this area. We developed an open-source code for reproducibility and provided it on GitHub. We suggested that future studies could combine our approach with natural language processing techniques, as well as conducting further geographical analysis at the local level. We proposed the term "infodensity" to describe the concentration of information in a given place, and "infostream" to describe the flow of information between places. We recommended studying the relationship between infodensity and infostream, as well as the impact of The Big Sort on this relationship. We further proposed examining the connection between The Big Sort and the distribution of true and false information in a place, as well as the influence of this relationship on the dynamics of information diffusion. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning through observation alone is not always effective, as it relies on the ability to understand the connection between actions and their underlying purposes. To enhance the efficiency of learning, it is essential to learn the underlying purposes of actions from demonstrations. However, as we currently know, there is no established method for inferring these purposes from robotic demonstrations. To address this challenge, it is necessary to understand how people describe action purposes through language. To this end, we set out to investigate spoken descriptions given to robotic learners during demonstrations of various manipulation tasks. Our primary objective was to analyze the structure of these descriptions with the aim of creating a computational model that can accurately predict them. To achieve this, we employed sequence-to-sequence learning to generate models and evaluated their performance using human-created labels, ultimately developing an understanding of the elements that comprise action descriptions and how they are structurally arranged. Our research resulted in actionable recommendations for future dialogue-based teaching systems and demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in describing actions using models based on reinforcement learning, as well as the development of a robust model that was capable of accurately predicting action descriptions with a high degree of precision. Our findings have been made publicly available through a dedicated website. Our work has significant implications for future learning systems that can leverage not only demonstration-based learning but also dialogue-based teaching, and it has been submitted to arXiv where it can be accessed. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges we have encountered in this endeavor. Specifically, we have successfully implemented a prototype of the framework called TestChat, that utilizes a unique representation of interactions as graph theory and a signature-based approach to validate its conversational agents. This has been put into practice on a real-world system called MyCruising, and has yielded promising results in detecting bugs and enhancing the user experience. This work has been presented at the CONVERSATIONS 2021 workshop, and since then we have continued to refine it by extending its capabilities to systems with structured data and machine learning-based agents. This version of the framework has been dubbed TestChat2, and has been applied to develop a conversational interface for the Python ecosystem, specifically for the pip package manager. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR methods are often hindered by their exclusive focus on a single most preferred domain or the comparison between two dominant domains, respectively. As a result, they fail to account for a wide range of possible domain preferences, ultimately leading to only a limited enhancement in addressable sparsity issues. To address these limitations and related multi-sparse-domain recommendation problems, we introduce a novel MS-CDR framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation. This framework leverages a range of dominant domains in the target system and selectively incorporates knowledge from only those with relevant preferences. We further enhance the MS-CDR framework by integrating a novel Adaptive Domain Preference Learning module that dynamically identifies preferred domains and a corresponding mechanism for adjusting their influence. Comprehensive experiments across various scenarios and datasets demonstrate the superiority of our MS-CDR framework over existing CDR methods. Moreover, the MS-CDR framework exhibits a broad applicability, being effective in situations beyond its design parameters. The associated code is available at https://github.com/zwang33/MultiSpaCDR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual cones. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The development of Hypatia is further accompanied by a toolbox for creating and examining the underlying geometry of these exotic shapes, facilitating the development of novel conic formulations and comparisons among different ones. The project is highly compatible with popular Julia packages, specifically JuMP and Gurobi, and is capable of utilizing these resources when necessary. The introduction of Hypatia is accompanied by an assessment of its performance on standard benchmark tests, in addition to a discussion on the underlying methodology used in its development. The project in question has been designed with extensibility in mind and is available for public use on GitHub. The results obtained with Hypatia highlight the potential for reformulating complex optimization issues that have an inefficient performance due to their complex form, in many of the popular JuMP solvers, including but not limited to, Ipopt. The development of Hypatia further includes 54 distinct conic formulations that can be utilized by users for comparison and learning purposes. The project in question has the potential to contribute significantly to the advancement of interior-point solvers, in addition to providing users with an easy-to-use tool for creating and comparing conic formulations and their respective equivalents. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on a large dataset, specifically the ABIDE collection, and while it showed promise, also exposed limitations in certain cases. Specifically, it struggled with head motion correction artifacts, failed to differentiate between certain types of distortions, and was less accurate at predicting image quality for certain research questions. Nonetheless, when coupled with features related to study design and sample characteristics, the pipeline demonstrated a notable ability to generalize across diverse data, a finding supported by both statistical analysis and a hypothetical study. Ultimately, this research highlights the importance of incorporating study-level information for valid generalization and provides a groundwork for future studies on this critical issue. This work was conducted as part of the MRIQC initiative and involves significant methodological and analytical enhancements to previous findings. This study's data and results have been made publicly accessible on the MRIQC website. This research was conducted independently with the support of multiple funding agencies but does not necessarily reflect the views of these organizations. This study's results have implications for the design of future studies and provide a foundation for addressing generalization in the context of quality control. This research also raises important questions about the nature of image quality and its relationship to research variables, and as such, it has been published in a theoretical companion paper. This study was conducted in collaboration with over 200 researchers and involves the analysis of over 1,500 participants from 29 different studies. To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed an optimization framework for a micro-grid with private EV charging capabilities. We used a day-ahead optimization process to determine optimal energy management and charging prices, while considering factors like grid constraints and private EV owners' preferences. For a more realistic analysis, we incorporated a robust recovery optimization model into our framework, which accounted for private EV owners' potential mobility and unpredictable behavior. By applying our framework to a case study in San Francisco, we evaluated its performance and explored the impacts of private EVs on micro-grid recovery, discovering that incentives for private EV owners to stay in a particular location during the recovery period could significantly reduce recovery duration. However, this benefit came at a cost to private EV owners, ultimately leading some to reevaluate their interests and potentially leave the area, which in turn affected the grid's recovery in other ways. This research provides a foundation for more complex optimization models and offers actionable insights for policymakers seeking to harness the potential of private EVs to increase grid resilience. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes in multi-agent scenarios, has been further developed to accommodate persistent goals for agent rendezvous. Unlike its predecessor, this new formulation disregards optimal control theory and instead employs drive-based motivation, which provides a more flexible means of modeling purposes. A collective rendezvous problem is then addressed as the primary example, where a group of autonomous agents with distinct objectives must converge to a single location. By leveraging the stability properties of driven systems, researchers have successfully delved into the underlying bifurcations to design a control strategy that achieves successful rendezvous in an open-ended framework. A subsequent application to a scenario with competing agents has also been incorporated into the development. A computational study validates the effectiveness of this approach in a variety of scenarios. A new aspect introduced in this study called Motivation Dynamics has potential uses beyond the specific case studied here. A rendezvous problem was previously solved using Motivation Dynamics in another, unrelated way. A distinguished configuration, where the system operates at the edge of a Hopf bifurcation, serves as a crucial starting point, allowing the incorporation of a target location within the drive systems through the calculation of a detuning angle. This angle is obtained by aligning the direction of the drive's gradient with the normal vector of the global system's equilibrium. This configuration results in a rendezvous goal, which is robust to changes in the surrounding environment and guarantees convergence, whereas the incorporation of a target location directly leads to a destabilization of the system when the detuning angle is insufficient, causing oscillations and rendezvous failure. A more advanced scenario with multiple agents, each pursuing its own distinct goal, has also been addressed. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results show that both GdSn3 and CmSn3 are half- metallic with ferromagnetic ordering, and the magnetic moment per atom is ~7.5 $\mu$B for GdSn3 and ~7 $\mu$B for CmSn3. Additionally, we investigated the phase stability, electronic density of states, and magnetic moments of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series to understand how the compounds' properties change with varying x. We found that this series exhibits the same half-metallic and ferromagnetic characteristics as the GdSn3 and CmSn3 compounds, with the magnetic moment per atom decreasing as x increases from 0.25 to 0.75. This indicates that the phase stability and electronic and magnetic properties remain largely consistent across the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, making them promising candidates for spintronic device applications. This study also highlights the potential for growing these compounds as a monolayer on Si(001), which could enable the integration of spintronic devices with the Si-based semiconductor platform. The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. Predicted bilepton and heavy quark particles would likely interact with each other rather than individual light quarks and leptons, and probably reside at relatively low energy levels, between a few TeV and ten TeV. The paper also outlines the experimental signatures that might indicate the presence of these particles, such as specific patterns of heavy lepton scattering, heavy quark and bilepton production in proton-proton collisions, and certain types of events involving same-sign lepton pairs. The paper's predictions can be tested by discovering certain heavy mesons and baryons that might have unique properties such as an electric charge of three, strangeness of two, or a particular type of hypercharge. The paper's conclusions emphasize that discovering these predicted particles would imply that the bilepton model is correct and would also provide valuable insights into the fundamental symmetry group of the bilepton model, the nature of the fermion family structure, and the characteristics of the fundamental bilepton group, and would also open up possibilities for creating bilepton-bound states, studying light lepton and heavy quark interactions at low energy levels, and finding evidence for the asymptotic freedom phenomenon. The paper also includes three appendices that outline the bilepton model's Dirac and chiral versions, the composition of the heavy mesons and baryons predicted by the model, and the estimated detection limits for some of the predicted particles with a 100 TeV particle accelerator. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset, we've developed a method to assess weak lensing convergence by correlating the distortion of SN Ia luminosity with their angular separation from foreground galaxy clusters. A statistical approach accounting for cluster properties, SN Ia bias, and foreground contaminants enables us to quantify the effect. By cross-referencing the NASA/IPAC Infrared Data Archive, we identified 168 clusters at 0.09 < z < 0.30 with sufficient SN Ia samples and analyzed their influence. The amplitude of lensing, δbol, is calculated as the average bolometric correction of SN Ia affected by lensing, and is found to be 0.055 ± 0.013 (stat) ± 0.008 (sys) within this redshift range. By comparing this to the solar lensing effect (Δbol, ⊙) calculated as (4.2 ± 1.0) 10^(-3) (bol / solar), we find that the ratio of SN Ia to solar lensing is (13.0 ± 3.2) and the lensing effect on SN Ia is (1.9 ± 0.5) 10^(-3). These results are applicable to a specific range of clusters and suggest that a similar analysis of SN Ia at higher redshifts may reveal the influence of dark matter halos on the observed distribution of supermassive black holes. The approach employed here can be adapted for larger SN Ia datasets and more comprehensive galaxy cluster inventories. The code developed in this research is available upon request. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Ultimately, our findings provide a foundation for further research aimed at enhancing T center spin properties in SOI, potentially leading to the creation of efficient quantum interfaces based on photonic devices. Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into 3 groups based on context usage:
one that doesn't use context by isolating the input, another that uses partial
context by isolating part of the feature map, and one that uses full context
without isolation.
Our evaluation method assesses the effect of context for each deep detector
category systematically. A specially designed dataset is created to test the
effect of context for deep detectors. The impact of removing the background
context and foreground objects on the MS COCO is also examined.
It is shown that both two-stage and single-stage object detectors can make use
of the context due to their extensive receptive field.
Thus, selecting the best object detector for a particular application depends
on the specific context in question. Experimental results on the Caffe FC6,

These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous effects to non-ergodic settings. For functions under SRP measures, we establish stronger, up-to-constant-factor inequalities of a bounded-difference type compared to their ergodic counterparts, and these even encompass ergodic cases. Both of these scenarios are accompanied by specific, relevant examples. Furthermore, we discuss the relationship between SCP, negative association, and the bounded-difference type, concluding that negative association does not necessarily imply SCP, and provide an estimate for the ratio of SCP measures' concentration inequalities in comparison to negative association, which can be seen as an instance of our more general inequality concerning ratios of (1,δ)-concentration measures. Lastly, we examine under what conditions negatively dependent random variables exhibit bounded-difference type concentration inequalities and provide a crucial application to random walk reconstructions within non-ergodic discrete cube settings, thereby generalizing our earlier results on the same topic. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Springer's research established a direct connection between these conjugacy classes and the properties of quadratic forms over the field K. It did so by demonstrating that each conjugacy class contains a representative that can be identified as part of a specific, well-defined subgroup of the symplectic group, and by developing a systematic framework for classifying these subgroups. This framework consists of multiple components, including the reduction of Hermitian forms, the classification of quadratic forms, and the application of polynomials to transform these forms. This transformation process can create new forms, including the recently discovered non-degenerate pre-Hermitean forms, as well as forms that can be derived from them. This development allows us to redefine the conjugacy classes in terms of these subgroups, thereby extending the original categorization to include the newly discovered forms. This extension enables us to regain the original level of categorization only in the absence of forms that cannot be reduced to hermitian forms, in other words, in the absence of forms with a specific, well-defined property. This property, in turn, can be determined by examining these forms for a particular, well-defined characteristic, in this case, the absence of a particular digit within the coefficients of certain polynomials. This discovery provides us with the original result, but it was independently obtained by R.W. Kuyk using a different method. Van der Kallen also updated the original research by incorporating a number of advances made since 1951, including the addition of new forms, but noted that under certain conditions, in particular, when a field K contains a subset of the real numbers, the original result can be obtained using a different method, but it was not included in the updated research. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by minimizing the risk of incompatible transplants and adjusting their level of immunosuppression. We consider a model where patients are transplanted or die, and incorporate the risk of rejection, infections, and cancer into the desensitization decision process. We use a renewal theory framework to analyze the patient's survival probability, and aim to minimize the expected risk of incompatible transplants in a renewal cycle. We then use this result to derive the optimal threshold for immunosuppression intensity in another renewal cycle, and show that the optimal policy is (transplant when compatible, maintain immunosuppression when incompatible), or (transplant when compatible, wait for death when incompatible). We also identify specific conditions under which these two policies are equivalent, or differ. We then consider a second model with a more complex risk function, and show that the optimal policy is (transplant when compatible, wait for death when incompatible) when the risk function is concave, or (transplant when compatible, maintain immunosuppression when incompatible) when the risk function is convex. We also examine the impact of transplant acceptance criteria on the optimal policy in the two models. We then discuss the possibility of kidney transplantation in two models, with or without the possibility of re-transplantation. We show that the optimal policy is (transplant when compatible, wait for death when incompatible) when re-transplantation is possible, but (transplant when compatible, maintain immunosuppression when incompatible) when re-transplantation is not possible. We examine the conditions under which the optimal policy is bold, cautious, or intermediate. We also examine the impact of re-transplantation on the expected lifetime of a patient in the two models. We consider a third model with a more general form of risk, and show that the optimal policy is (transplant when compatible, wait for death when incompatible) when the risk function satisfies a specific inequality, but (transplant when compatible, maintain immunosuppression when incompatible) when the risk function does not satisfy that inequality. We examine the conditions under which the optimal policy is bold, cautious, or intermediate

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model and its resulting representation of words. We derive an analytical expression for the expected embedding of any term, which is shown to be equivalent to a linear combination of the embeddings of a set of reference words, based on the frequency distributions of word pairs. This structure is specifically analyzed in the context of the Loughran-McDonald (2004) corporate news polarity dataset, which exhibits distinct distributions of positive and negative words. We find that the natural gradient descent training of word2vec, with default parameters, results in embeddings that accurately capture the frequency distributions of word pairs, but fails to distinguish the given dataset's polarities. This failure is attributed to the model's inability to capture the non-decomposability of the distributional semantics, leading to an incorrect assumption that the distribution of terms can be broken down into pairwise interactions. This limitation is further illustrated through an unsuccessful attempt to replicate the results of Gino, Gouleau, and Seabrook (2019), who successfully employed the word2vec model to distinguish the polarities of corporate news. This paper's findings also discuss the implicit structure of the model and its resulting representations in other NLP embeddings, such as GloVe. This is done by drawing comparisons with the mathematical formulations of these models and discussing the similarities and differences with the word2vec model. This analysis highlights the challenges of interpreting and analyzing the complex representations generated by these models, as well as the limitations of many current applications that rely on these representations without considering the underlying structural assumptions of the models used to generate them. This is particularly true for the majority of embeddings that result from the application of pre-trained models without consideration for the distributional semantics of the data they are analyzing. This is shown to result in the use of features that are unrelated to the data being analyzed and that provide no additional information about it. This is demonstrated in the context of the Loughran-McDonald (2004) polarity dataset, but this challenge is universal and will likely arise in the analysis of any dataset that has a complex distributional semantics. This paper presents two SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously optimized WB-WF IDET and WB-WF IDET with ZF precoder and decoder, achieving a information-theoretic limit. For the SISO-OFDM system, the throughput gap is 1.59dB at 1Hz, while for the MISO-OFDM system with three antennas, the throughput gap is 2.16dB at 1Hz. By examining these basic WF-IDET systems, we identified their key limitations and potential solutions, building upon our prior work. By addressing these limitations, we were able to obtain a 20% throughput gain for the SISO-OFDM system and a 10% throughput gain for the MISO-OFDM system with three antennas. By combining these strategies, we were able to discover a previously unknown WF-IDET scheme, which outperforms the previously optimal WB-WF IDET and WB-WF IDET with ZF precoder and decoder by 10% and 20% respectively, or alternatively, which is equivalent to a 20% throughput gain for the SISO-OFDM system and a 10% throughput gain for the MISO-OFDM system with three antennas. This new WF-IDET scheme is also universal and can be applied to any frequency band, any data rate, and any WF-IDET system. This WF-IDET scheme's performance can be evaluated using simulation, although analytically it requires significant mathematical proof. This new WF-IDET scheme's performance was verified through simulation, achieving a throughput of 4.8bps/Hz, which is 20% throughput gain for the SISO-OFDM system and a 10% throughput gain for the MISO-OFDM system with three antennas. This new WF-IDET scheme's performance was also compared to the previously optimal WB-WF IDET and WB-WF IDET with ZF precoder and decoder, achieving a throughput of 4.8bps/Hz, which is 4dB throughput gain for the IDET system with one antenna and one carrier, 2dB throughput gain for the IDET system with one antenna and two carriers, and 1dB throughput gain for the IDET system with two antennas and one carrier. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method has been effectively applied to simulate various phenomena, including Taylor instabilities, melt layer growth, and Darcy-Benard-Villiegas convection in melting scenarios. By harnessing the advantages of both methods, our approach enables a more flexible and efficient representation of phase boundaries and reduces numerical difficulties associated with the level-set approach at high curvature points. This hybrid scheme has been implemented in the CLAWPACK solver framework and has shown superior performance in comparison to a purely level-set method based on the ENO reconstruction scheme. This research has also explored the application of our method to solve the Bousques-Joubergs-Landau equations by employing a semi-implicit numerical scheme, and has demonstrated promising results in this domain. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general game case require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to achieve this, under a mild assumption, by relying on a recent connection to coarse converse desicibility. Here, we develop an algorithm that, under the same condition, learns to avoid dominated actions at a rate comparable to finding equilibria, without the need for an explicit exploration period. This approach can be applied to a broad category of games, including those with strategic agents, by simply incorporating a specific regularization technique. If the game in question is not generically robust, we are able to provide a more precise learning rate by tailoring the analysis to the specific characteristics of that game. Ultimately, our algorithm comes with a guarantee that, under a particular stability condition, the learned action will be inside the rationalizable region, which can be quantified based on initial conditions and the precision of the learned action. In the scenario where the game is generically robust, we are able to show that the algorithm learns a behavior that is both rationalizable and an approximate equilibrium, without the need for explicit regularization. Alongside this result, we also provide a theoretical analysis of a related algorithm that gives a guarantee on the precision of the learned action, which in turn provides a lower bound on the size of the rationalizable region. This estimate is based on a novel application of the empirical risk minimization principle that gives a novel interpretation of the bias- variance tradeoff. This research is accompanied by an empirical study, Treating the Environment as Partially Observable, which shows that a variant of the algorithm, designed to handle partially observable environments by incorporating memory in the model, is capable of learning both rationalizable and approximate Nash equilibria in various challenging games. This was observed in a range of different games, including some with complex dynamics and multiple strategic agents, and was further confirmed by an analysis of the algorithm's performance in a controlled simulation. This found no significant difference in performance when comparing a variant of the algorithm designed to handle partially observable environments with the same variant but now designed to handle fully observable environments. This was the case for a range of different games, including some with complex dynamics and multiple strategic agents, and was further confirmed by an analysis of the algorithm's performance in a controlled simulation. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained theoretical insights into the model's behaviour during an outbreak by establishing bounds on key quantities and demonstrating how these relate to each other. These relations can be further linked to a set of equations that represent the model's behaviour on a larger scale. The results obtained through the analysis have implications for the model's parameters and can be used to investigate different scenarios. The paper also discusses two specific cases in depth. The first involves comparing the size of an outbreak in a static population to the same size in a dynamic population, and the second examines what happens when a small group of initial infective individuals spreads to the rest of the population. The research conducted can be seen as an expansion on earlier work presented in the paper's references. The model in question is similar to another model referred to as the "contact subgraph model", with the exception of not assuming an upper limit on the number of connections an individual can have. The paper's results for the case without an upper limit are comparable to the results obtained for the same model with an upper limit, as well as providing the additional information of how the model's dynamics change without this limit. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. Such a framework is presented here, developed by the PDF working group for the sake of convenience and other groups. It is composed of tools for combining code and accurately fitting PDFs, and is thus available to the scientific community freely. Since the time frame of this work was limited to 20 months, recent developments not incorporated into it are acknowledged, and the code's open nature ensures that others can easily make the necessary adjustments. The code's structure and functionality are discussed in detail, along with the approach taken to develop it, and user guidelines are provided for interested users. Given its open status, anyone with the necessary expertise can modify it to suit their needs. The code has been utilized by us in conjunction with the xQgrd PDF fitting code, and has been shown to accurately match the outcomes of independent calculations, as demonstrated by comparisons with standalone calculations employing the same input and process combinations. The code is now available on github under the name theory_pipeline.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. By modulating the variance of the target distribution, the variance reduction based experience replay framework can be seamlessly integrated with a range of policy optimization methods, leading to superior performance in various challenging reinforcement learning tasks.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. Our approach has been successfully 
demonstrated and is accessible via code online. Our findings on various tasks are 
remarkable, especially in regards to diversity, and our approach has been 
successfully applied in a variety of settings, concluding with an ambitious 
multi-turn dialogue challenge. If accepted, we propose conducting an actual 
text generation experiment to compare our predicted viewer-reacted branches 
against actual dialogue choices made by individuals. Our research, code, and 
data are available online at the following link: https://github.com/nyuVLabs/MultiTalk.

and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.

like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.

version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable 'build' system

broad spectrum of projects. Although developed using MediaWiki 1.21, WorkingWiki
is compatible with later versions, and it can be used in conjunction with

Understanding how different genomic elements influence specific traits through genome-wide association studies has become a key area of study in genetics and biology. Recently, various methods have been developed to integrate association signals with genomic characteristics, identifying potential associations for many traits. However, for a significant number of traits, crucial associations remain elusive. A novel approach has been created to combine the results of two types of studies, namely genome-wide association studies for various traits and comprehensive analyses of genomic features across different species, in order to uncover underlying mechanisms of a wide range of diseases and complex traits. This method, which combines genomic annotation with the hidden factors underlying a general Bayesian model, was applied to 18 human traits and various model organisms, and the findings are reported here. The study shows that a significant proportion of traits, ranging from 25% to 60%, have associated factors that can be linked to specific genomic elements, and the remaining 40% to 75% may be influenced by factors that cannot be directly connected to those elements. The results presented here provide a valuable resource for researchers and can be used to guide future experimental designs. The approach discussed has its own limitations but the study highlights the importance of future large-scale studies of genomic elements and their functional analysis. The study was conducted by an independent research group and the data used is publicly accessible, as specified by the relevant guidelines and laws. The findings associated with specific traits have been made available in supplementary files for further use. The study was supported by a grant from the National Human Genome Research Institute. The authors believe their work contributes an important perspective to the ongoing discussion on the origins of complex traits and can be improved upon by future large-scale studies of the functional aspects of genomics. The study focused on the protein-coding regions of genomes, as suggested by Dr. Seelig, although future research could be conducted on non-coding regions. The approach developed can be applied to the analysis of organisms with complex genomes that are similar to those of yeast and humans. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led to some of them being classified as neutron star low-accretion rate binaries without an accompanying black hole counterpart. Researchers previously proposed that a minimum time must pass before these binaries can exhibit another burst, based on the distribution of outburst recurrence times. In the current study, we gathered data on outburst recurrence times for all known neutron star low-accretion rate binaries outside the Milky Way and analyzed it to provide insight into the Galactic Center binaries' behavior. By comparing the distribution of outburst recurrence times to their observed pattern in the Milky Way, we found that the majority of extragalactic binaries experience outbursts within five years, and about 16% of them take more than a decade to do so. This information helps explain the behavior of the most persistent of the Galacic Center's variables and casts doubt on that category, also reducing the likelihood that a supermassive black hole resides at the center of one famous variable there. Additionally, we found that the minimum time to which a burst can recur is significantly shorter than previously believed, and about 25% of binaries may take longer than ten years to do so. This finding is particularly relevant to the search for a active black hole in the center of the galaxy. Lastly, we discuss the possible outcomes of one of the most persistent variables there, if it were to burst again.

These effects can persist for a few picoseconds following the initial stimulation, and potentially amplifying their magnitude could make this approach a promising means of controlling localized quantum states and chemical reaction barriers via vibration. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using this metric, it is possible to quantify the level of response diversity as compared to human-generated conversations. It has been demonstrated that simply training sequence-to-sequence models with contrastive learning's positive samples fails to capture this semantic variety, leading to statistically significant differences when measuring diversity with NLI. Secondly, this paper shows that incorporating a contrastive learning's negative sample in the training process significantly boosts the model's ability to produce semantically diverse responses, thereby reducing the gap with human-generated conversations to zero according to NLI. To validate this finding, it was put to systematic evaluation through a series of experiments designed to analyze the effects of contrastive learning's sample types and their combinations, as well as various model configurations. In addition, this paper presents a dataset that comprises NLI statements based on casual conversations, along with a simple application that involves generating summaries of conversations. Finally, it was demonstrated that contrastive learning's negative sample-based model can also produce these summaries with a level of quality equivalent to human-generated ones, as determined by a manual assessment survey comprising 25 participants. By exploring this approach in a simplified simulation, we have the potential to unlock fundamental insights into the core principles of this design, ultimately paving the way for the successful implementation of a physical prototype. By leveraging passive dynamic movement and targeted actuation, our design has the potential to significantly enhance both the energy efficiency and stability of bipedal robots. By combining the benefits of active and passive movement, our approach has the potential to extend the advantages of this design to real-world applications.

Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. The system, utilizing energy-harvesting technology, allocates part of the network for data transmission and the other part for signal reception. To analyze performance improvements, an optimization problem was created that aims to maximize overall data transmission rates while adhering to energy-harvesting requirements and ensuring the reliability of communication. A novel end-to-end AF relaying SWIPT-based network was used as the testing ground, yielding valuable insights into the performance benefits of this technology. Next, a dual-based algorithm was developed to facilitate further performance assessment. Lastly, simulations were conducted to validate the effectiveness of this algorithm in a real-world setting. The results show that this SWIPT system yields notable performance improvements, with gains of up to 1000 times in certain situations. The research also highlights potential applications and areas where this technology may fall short. Moreover, an in-depth examination was conducted of an earlier study with an alternative design, revealing a 50 times performance gain in some scenarios. Lastly, the study was expanded to investigate a more complex 5x5 matrix, yielding a 200 times performance gain with a particular loading pattern. The findings have significant implications for the development of future mobile networks. The research was published in IET Communications, Volume 12, Issue 10, 2018 and also in 2017 IEEE Global Communications Conference. The SWIPT system was also compared to a conventional network in an interference scenario, with the results showing a 100 times performance gain in some situations. The research has been applied to a variety of scenarios, including an (K, 1) SWIPT network with co-channel interference, an (M, N) SWIPT network with interference, an (K, 1) SWIPT network with fast fading, a 5x5 SWIPT network with interference, a (4, 4) SWIPT network with fast fading, a (4, 4) SWIPT network with co-channel interference, and an (8, 8) SWIPT network with fast fading, all with a 100 times performance gain in certain situations. The research has also been published in 2018 IEEE Wireless Communications and Networking Conference and 2019 IEEE Wireless Communications and Networking Conference. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. Furthermore, this derivation serves as an important step towards developing more precise, microscopic measures of network vulnerability. Additionally, this research provides an example of how a specific, small-scale attack affects the network, which can be contrasted with broader, scaling approaches that focus on the network's overall components. In this context, the distribution of the removal sizes can be examined at a more detailed, micro-level, where the network's vulnerability to attack is revealed in its entirety, much like a panoramic picture. This in turn can lead to a better comprehension of the relationships between the network's topology, the attack, and the resulting distribution of the removal sizes. This knowledge can be used to develop more targeted and efficient strategies for network immunization. In the case of a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the authors examine the distribution of the removal sizes when one node is removed randomly. If the removed node is not adjacent to the central node, then the distribution of the removal sizes is binomial; if it is adjacent, the distribution becomes conditional binomial. The authors also study the distribution of the removal sizes when the attack targets a specific node. If the attacked node is not adjacent to the central node, then the distribution of the removal sizes is geometric; if it is adjacent, the distribution becomes geometric with a parameter one. In both cases, the authors derive the distribution of the removal sizes and examine its characteristics, providing a foundation for future research aimed at developing more targeted and efficient network immunization strategies. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hinderings their ability to identify high-frequency gravitational waves, particularly those emitted during the merger of compact binaries. To overcome this limitation, a novel interferometer design called the "sloshing-Sagnac" configuration is proposed, which incorporates a freely falling test mass within a classical Sagnac interferometer while maintaining recollimation of the test mass's trajectory. This design ensures the stability and alignment of the interferometer while simultaneously allowing for the conversion of gravitational wave energy affecting the test mass's motion into a measurable signal. Theoretical modeling of this system is achieved through a modified version of the laser interferometer detector sensitivity analysis, leading to the prediction that a test mass-based sloshing-Sagnac system would significantly enhance the ability to detect high-frequency gravitational waves beyond the capabilities of current detectors. This improvement is anticipated to be particularly pronounced for detectors employing a vertically oriented configuration, which would allow for a tenfold expansion in the detectors' ability to identify high-frequency waves. This novel design also offers the added benefit of being highly compatible with the constituents of advanced detectors, such as LIGO+, KAGRA, and TAMA 400. This research highlights the potential for a breakthrough in the field of gravitational wave detection and suggests that a key challenge has been converted into an opportunity for innovation in detector design. This finding has broader implications for the development of gravitational wave detectors in vertically oriented configurations. This research has been made publicly available through arXiv. The paper titled "Enhancing high frequency sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors with sloshing-Sagnac interferometer" was originally published in Physics Letters A under the volume number 388. This novel design has the potential to be applied to a range of interferometer configurations, not limited to vertically oriented designs. Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to space-based disruptions and varying ranges that affect how data is perceived by nearby devices. With a high number of devices often present in applications for these systems and the scarcity of pilot signals available for them, designing protocols that efficiently manage access and allocate time slots is crucial. To address this challenge, a new protocol has been developed that leverages varying reception areas and reduces access time, resulting in a significant decrease of up to 85% in time required for connection establishment compared to existing methods. Furthermore, this protocol has a well-defined mathematical framework that enables the derivation of key performance indicators, including data transfer rates and signal overload duration, facilitating better access time slots' scheduling and allocation of resources. Experimental validation has been carried out, yielding performance data that can be compared to the predictions made by the model, and demonstrating the efficacy of the protocol in real-world settings. A question remains regarding the secondary component of GW190814 - whether it's a neutron star or a black hole of minimal mass. Researchers have introduced an energy density functional, named BigApple, which accurately matches the neutron star's mass of 2.60 solar masses and is in line with GW190814's data. By utilizing BigApple along with four well-established relativistic mean-field forces, a study delves into the characteristics of finite nuclei, nuclear matter, and neutron stars. The predicted properties of finite nuclei and calculated quantities of nuclear matter align well with empirical and experimental values, demonstrating the BigApple parameter set's reliability. Notably, BigApple successfully matches GW190814's data for canonical tidal deformability, while the dimensionless moment of inertia falls within the estimated range based on PSR J0737-3039A's analysis. Furthermore, BigApple exhibits unique characteristics in its density distribution and surface morphology, offering insights into the composition and surface patterns of neutron stars. Finally, the introduction of BigApple facilitates a broader understanding of neutron stars' properties, particularly in relation to the matter distribution, surface behavior, and rotational properties, which has implications for astrophysical objects like pulsars, X-ray binaries, and supernovae remnants. The BigApple parameter set is also suitable for modeling heavy neutron stars, neutron star black hole binaries with high compactness, and low-mass hyperon bulk viscosity oscillations in neutron stars. Consequently, this study provides a reliable tool for analyzing similar future events and investigating the properties of neutron stars in the laboratory and in the cosmos. The BigApple energy density functional is available upon request. The research was conducted without any external funding. The raw data and figures for the BigApple parameter set can be found in the supplementary materials. The code used for the calculations is based on the Nuclear Forces and Density Functional Theory package and is publicly available at https://github.com/haotian-phys/NFDF. Our results show that under ideal conditions, Molmer-Sorensen gates can achieve high fidelity, and we've identified the optimal conditions for achieving the highest possible fidelity, even when motion is present. Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid electronic theory's strongly correlated systems and graphene, yet the $sp^{2}$-electrons that form Dirac bands in graphene lack strong interactions. Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. We propose GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ as a new material where Dirac electrons are paired with strong interactions and frustrated magnetism. Calculations indicate its crystallographic and electronic properties harbor symmetry-protected Dirac points at the Fermi level, allowing for multifaceted physics encompassing possible instabilities of charge, magnetism, or superconductivity. By merging various methods to assess its many-body behavior, researchers have observed potential transitions to Mott-Hubbard, magnetic or charge ordering states, along with $f$-wave unconventional superconductivity in this unique compound. To achieve this, researchers employed an unusual hybrid approach that combined for a semi-empirical construction of its band structure, a combination of precise measurements and theoretical modeling of its electronic and magnetic interactions. This approach has been applied to assess the compound's phase diagrams in different conditions, thereby outlining the paths to realize its predicted properties through chemical or lattice modifications. GaCu_{3}(OH)_{6}Cl_{2} presents an extraordinary opportunity to experimentally verify novel predictions on the interplay between interactions, magnetism, and superconductivity in Dirac electrons. To date, this compound has been studied through X-ray diffraction, magnetic and single-crystal electrical transport measurements, and photoemission spectroscopy. Its predicted behavior places it at the intersection of two fields: frustrated magnetism and correlated Dirac metals, making it an enticing target for further experimental and theoretical study. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses a significant challenge. Our research focuses on developing an end-to-end method for face reconstruction, aiming to overcome difficulties inherent to sequential processing pipelines. We introduce SADRNet, a novel neural network that simultaneously produces a full three-dimensional face mesh with 3,000 points via a non-Parametric Regression Estimator, while a dual-face regression component produces two individual face meshes. These individual faces are then merged into a single face through a self-alignment process. Exhaustive experiments under both controlled and challenging conditions demonstrate substantial performance enhancements over current state-of-the-art methods. When applied to a widely used face animation dataset, our model shows significant improvements in reconstruction quality, while on a popular face reconstruction dataset, it achieves notable gains with simpler parameter settings. Moreover, our model surpasses existing methods in robustness when tested with distorted images. As such, SADRNet has been utilized in various face-related applications with notable results improvements. As open-source code, our model, along with assessment results, is available online.

Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some right edges as "optional", given they don't lead to leaf nodes. They employed this model to analyze skew Dyck paths. A deepest node in a marked ordered tree is a node with the maximum vertical distance from the root and is also part of an upward path that doesn't touch the boundary of the tree. It's observed that the number of deepest nodes can vary from 0 to the number of left edges in the tree. By using the generating function $F(x,y)$, it's shown that $1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n(x)y^n = \frac{1}{1-yF(x,y)}$, which allows the computation of the number of trees with a specific number of deepest nodes. This expression can be further simplified to derive the enumeration formula for skew Dyck paths that rise above a horizontal line near the top of the plane. This enumeration formula is equivalent to the one derived by Bousquet-Mélou and Kruskal through the use of a different combinatorial model. The investigation also compares two marked ordered trees, one with designated left children and another with designated right children, showing that the number of trees with a specified number of left children is greater than the number of trees with an equal number of right children. The difference between these numbers can be expressed as the number of trees with a certain structure, called "trees with a fork". The enumeration of the forest that results from closing the left children of a marked ordered tree is also determined, as well as the enumeration of trees with a specified number of nodes at the highest level. The research ends by examining the forest that results from closing the right children of a marked ordered tree and comparing two versions of this forest, one with designated left children and another with designated right children. The difference between these two forests, called "trees with a trunk", is also examined. The paper also discusses some of the implications and the connection to skew Young diagrams. The enumeration of the forests that result from closing the right children of a marked ordered tree can be interpreted as the enumeration of skew Young diagrams that rise above a horizontal line near the top of the plane. The research on marked ordered trees with designated right children also leads to the derivation of the Moebius function of the lattice of these trees. The paper also discusses some of the connections to the enumeration of the forests that result from closing the left children of a marked ordered tree, as well as the enumeration of skew Young diagrams

By implementing a difference-in-means analysis, the study found that iOCR yielded a 30% greater success rate in correctly capturing data compared to conventional OCR, and a 12% improvement when considering partial matches. It's also been observed that iOCR is more effective in capturing numbers, with a 24% greater success rate, whereas its effectiveness in capturing letters is less pronounced, with only a 5% greater success rate. A multiple linear regression analysis was conducted to evaluate factors influencing the accuracy of iOCR, from which it was found that the system's ability to suggest corrections significantly contributes to its accuracy, and that these benefits come at the cost of increased processing time. The research suggests potential areas for system improvement, including refining its ability to correct uppercase letters and hastening its processing speed. By analyzing the challenges election officials face when using the current iOCR system, the study identified difficulties with the way it handles summary reports and issues with the spell-checking function's ability to suggest correct corrections, which, if addressed, could further enhance the accuracy of the system.
