The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated that surface roughness causes disruption of the foam structure, resulting in increased friction. By distinguishing between the causes of disrupted structure (interface disruption) and roughness (interface disruption), we have shown that the interface disruption leads to friction. By focusing on this disruption, we were able to determine the stress it causes and found it to be directly related to the stress caused by the contact angle of the liquid. By incorporating this stress into our model, we were able to accurately predict the resulting friction. This prediction can be applied to a wide range of flows, from slow movements to rapid deformations, by modeling the interface disruption as a source of stress that contributes to the flow's resistance. This research provides a fundamental understanding of the flow of liquid foams and the importance of considering the stress caused by the disruption of interfaces in contact with surfaces, a principle that can be applied to other complex liquids in similar situations. This knowledge can be further utilized to modify our model of flow within liquid foams, as well as other complex liquids that behave in a similar manner. This model, in turn, can be used to better understand the flow of liquid foams by comparing our stress measurements with a newly developed non-local regularization model, which provides a more detailed visual representation of the deformations occurring within the foam. This representation can be obtained through the simulation of our stress measurements, as well as the removal of air bubbles from surfaces, which is an important phenomenon in its own right. This research has also shown that the flow of liquid foams can be distinguished from the flow of other complex liquids, such as emulsions, by visualizing the deformations of individual air bubbles, which cannot be achieved through stress measurements alone. This finding has significant implications for understanding the flow of liquid emulsions, which behave in a similar manner to liquid foams but with oil bubbles instead of air bubbles. This research has also demonstrated that surface roughness can cause the breakdown of interfaces and lead to friction, which has a direct relationship with the stress caused by the contact angle of the liquid. This knowledge can be applied to a wide range of flows, both within and outside of the field of complex liquids, which behave in a similar manner to liquid foams. The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, has been examined in a study that also compared its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computations that accounted for both curvature and tension-driven forces revealed that the membrane's shape conformed to a conical finger, while beyond a certain critical curvature, the resulting pattern transformed into a radial finger. Inextensibility led to an increase in the size of the developed finger, whereas extreme inextensibility resulted in the formation of a grid-like pattern; in contrast, the difference brought about by the elasticity was relatively minor. The distinct patterns that emerged were highly dependent on the rate of rotation, outer pressure, and difference in fluid densities. The study also discovered that the size of the developed finger could be described by a non-dimensional group of rotating Rayleigh-Taylor instability that included the effects of curvature, tension, and rotation, thus providing a framework for comparing it with similar non-rotating scenarios. The study further found that the border between the radial and conical fingers was highly sensitive to the rate of rotation, unlike the situation in a non-rotating Hele-Shaw cell. The distinctive patterns that formed in the center of the cell could extend radially outward, varying with the rate of rotation, while the size of the developed finger decreased with an increase in the outer pressure and the difference in fluid densities, and could also be influenced by the curvature of the cell walls, and had all been captured in the results' graphs. The research involved an examination of the effects of the elasticity of the membrane, the rate of rotation, the difference in fluid densities, the outer pressure, and the curvature of the cell walls on the patterns of the developed fingers, and had compared the inextensibility of the membrane to its extreme elasticity, and had derived a set of non-dimensional groups governing the behavior of the system. The study had also found that the patterns formed in the rotating Hele-Shaw cell were distinct from those formed in a non-rotating Hele-Shaw cell, and had provided a set of non-dimensional groups that could describe the behavior of the system in a Hele-Shaw cell of any curvature.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 3-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. Isotope measurements allow for the determination of ethynyl cyclopentadiene's total abundance, with results indicating its column density is roughly 7 times greater than cyclopentadiene's, and both are about 30 times more abundant than methyl cyclopentadiene. Furthermore, the newly discovered isomers have a similar abundance ratio to each other, with the 1-ethynyl form being approximately 1.5 times more abundant than the 3-ethynyl form. Isotopic measurements of the ethynyl group yield a relative abundance of 1400±140 for CCH over CN within the TMC-1 direction, which is comparable to previous findings, and both have a similar abundance to cyclopentadiene and methyl cyclopentadiene. Isotopic measurements of the diatomic groups also enable the derivation of relative abundances for specific hydrocarbon derivatives, with results showing that the most abundant are CH, CCH, and CN, whereas the ethynyl methyl, cyclopropenyl, and cyclopentadiene derivatives are significantly less abundant, with the latter two being approximately 30 times less abundant than the most abundant. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/ruishanwu/PyTorch-look-ahead-attention.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in areas like artificial intelligence, network security, and biomedical research could fuel similar interdisciplinary developments. We examine the history of grid computing as an example of this kind of development, highlighting the importance of a translational approach that bridges the gap between complex technologies and practical applications. By deconstructing the components of this approach, we can provide a framework for other developments in this field. This paper also presents theoretical constructs, such as the Biomedical Informatics Triangle, that can be applied to other areas outside of biomedical research. We discuss the various forms that a translational grid computing community could take and offer guidance on establishing and maintaining such a community. Finally, we discuss the challenges of evaluating and measuring progress in this kind of development, using the development of grid computing as a case study. We conclude by exploring the potential for a new generation of innovations that could arise from a future era of technological disparity. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. By numerically simulating the model, we find that it yields a result indistinguishable from $\Lambda$CDM, both in terms of its effect on the cosmic expansion history and in its impact on the evolution of matter density clusters. Our results also demonstrate that the model can effectively bridge the era of matter-dominated cosmology by adopting a specific exponent, without the need for an abrupt transition. This is particularly evident when comparing its effects on the evolution of the Hubble parameter and the density of clusters to those predicted by $\Lambda$CDM. This is an important distinction from the exponential models commonly found in the literature. This model offers a versatile tool for simulating various cosmological scenarios, while its parameters have a clear physical meaning. This is in contrast to models that rely on the phenomenological coefficients of polynomials, without any direct connection to the model's asymptotic behavior. This model can also be used to examine the onset of the era dominated by dark energy, which we find occurs when the distance variable exceeds approximately one. This is in agreement with the conventional understanding that the universe became dominated by dark energy at a redshift of one. This model can be used in a variety of contexts, ranging from the study of the early universe to its late stages, as well as in the analysis of the structure of the universe and the formation of the cosmic web. This is in addition to providing an accurate estimate for the age of the universe, which is found to be $13.8$ Gyr, a value that is in agreement with the results obtained using the Planck satellite. This value for the age of the universe is derived without the need to include the parameter that accounts for the degree of viscososity in the model, as this parameter has a negligible impact on the time it takes for the universe to reach its current stage. We analyzed the J/ψ particle's ability to decay into invisible matter by considering various neutrino and dark matter scenarios and compared our results with existing data, concluding that such a process must occur at a rate lower than a certain value if another phenomenon is to be explained. We also determined that even if J/ψ's ability to decay into invisible matter is significantly reduced, it would still occur at a certain frequency. Furthermore, we discussed the implications of these findings for future experiments that could detect the J/ψ particle and potentially other particles that can also decay into invisible matter. This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience. The package includes example use cases, including the aforementioned temperature and vegetation datasets, along with guidance on implementing MFSSA for user-defined problems. The R package and algorithm documentation are accessible at https://github.com/kuo-lab/Rfssa. The Rfssa R package can be installed directly using the command install.packages("Rfssa"). The Rfssa R package is available on CRAN at https://cran.r-project.org/package=Rfssa. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and it is powered by 13.56 MHz RF energy. Despite its fundamental principle, based on whether it is driven in a helical or axial mode, it was unclear how plasma was generated in the IShTAR chamber. A study was conducted to understand this process, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle composition, and it confirmed that plasma is created through a helicon process rather than a magnetized electron layer. This was supported by the presence of a strong magnetic field perpendicular to the RF wave, as well as observations of a specific plasma density oscillation, and it has significant implications for future upgrades of the device. A second modification to the device, already in progress, will involve replacing the plasma source with a longer helicon discharge chamber, which is expected to produce a more consistent plasma profile, necessary for investigating how plasma interacts with waves in a helicon mode. This will require the power of the RF generator to be increased, which poses a significant technical challenge. This issue could be addressed by switching to a different helicon mode, but it requires a more complex analysis, which has not been conducted as part of this study. This analysis has been performed and it showed that there are multiple helicon modes possible, which could be relevant for similar devices used in other areas, such as space plasma studies, cancer treatment, and material processing. This study involved the use of a multi-species plasma fluid model, which provided a detailed explanation of the electron and ion energy distribution functions, as well as the formation of a helicon mode in the IShTAR device. This model also enabled the prediction of the necessary modifications to extend the helicon mode to higher frequencies, which could be relevant for other devices. This study demonstrated the effectiveness of a helicon discharge plasma source, which could serve as a model for similar devices used in other areas, and it provided a framework for analyzing and predicting the behavior of these devices. This framework could be applied to future upgrades of the IShTAR device, other similar devices, as well as other plasma devices used in cancer treatment, material processing, and space plasma studies. This study also highlighted the importance of considering the interaction between the magnetic field and the RF wave, which could be relevant for other devices

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. A subsequent examination of a GCNN applied to a linear classification task reveals the underlying principles and features that it learns, demonstrating how GCNNs effectively generalize compared to traditional Neural Networks. A software implementation of our explanation is also provided, allowing readers to experiment with different configurations and models. A performance comparison between a general Neural Network and the same network presented in a GCNN form shows that they exhibit similar accuracy levels, whereas a comparison with a standard CNN revealed that our GCNN equivalent had a 6.01% lower accuracy, indicating that our analysis may serve as a foundation for future optimization and improvement of GCNNs. A numerical illustration of a more complex graph convolutional network is also presented, along with its software implementation. A discussion on the implications of our analysis for the selection of hyperparameters and the optimization of GCNNs is also provided. A hypothetical GCNN designed to recognize the patterns in the well-known MNIST dataset is proposed, along with its software implementation, and a comparison with a standard Neural Network revealed that our GCNN had a 5.65% lower accuracy, suggesting that our analysis may serve as a foundation for future optimization and improvement of GCNNs. A discussion on the limitations of our analysis and its potential applications for the training of GCNNs and the derivation of hyperparameters is also presented. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding, axial displacement is generally measured with high precision due to its direct correlation with backscatter data, whereas measuring lateral displacement is more challenging because it is indirectly inferred from axial displacement. Several studies have explored new synthetic aperture ultrasound techniques with little impact on displacement measurement accuracy, while others, like the Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) technique, are thought to have a more significant impact but remain untested for their effect on accuracy. This study investigates the VSSA technique's impact on lateral displacement measurement, comparing its results with the widely accepted method known as Full-Differential elastography. Experimental data from 20 ex-vivo bovine liver samples with varying lipid inclusion percentages are used in this study, with each sample scanned five times. The results show that the VSSA technique yields more accurate measurements of both axial and lateral displacement, leading to a 34% improvement in accuracy over the widely accepted method known as Full-Differential elastography. This finding suggests that the VSSA technique can be used to enhance the elastography technique. This study further investigates the VSSA technique's effect on accuracy when used with a spatially distributed aperture, finding that its effect is minimal when the distribution is wide. This research also introduces two novel assessment metrics, assigns a value of 0.034 to the Widin index, and assigns a value of 0.13 to the Coefficient of Variance, which are used to evaluate the elastography technique's accuracy. This study's findings have the potential to guide ultrasound elastography technique development by providing the VSSA technique and its associated assessment frameworks as tools to enhance the technique's accuracy. This research demonstrates the VSSA technique's effectiveness in elastography, but also shows that it is not suitable for scanning distributed soft tissues. This study further explores the technique's effectiveness in scanning distributed soft tissues by introducing the Synthetic Aperture Based Virtual Source (SABVS) technique, which aims to overcome the limitations of the VSSA technique. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. Our analysis also delves into the relationship between natural deduction and natural gamma calculus, demonstrating the equivalence between the two systems. Furthermore, this equivalence enables us to translate natural deduction into natural gamma calculus, providing a straightforward method for converting first-order natural deduction proofs into sequent calculus proofs. This conversion can be applied to validate the correctness of lambda terms against types, as well as to derive type inference for lambda terms based on natural deduction proofs. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. We surpass the former bounds of [Cohen-Steiner et al. '09 and Har-Peled et al. '10] by achieving the optimal storage term for $k$ and near-optimal storage for high-dimensional data. Furthermore, we derive a pairwise-distance coreset with a storage of $k$ polynomial dimensions, shedding light on the underlying structure of the problem. As a result of these coreset structures, we can efficiently solve the clustering problem in the streaming setting by means of a variety of techniques, including optimality for the $(1\pm c_\Delta)$-approximation for any given $c_\Delta$ or $0 < c_\Delta < 1$, dynamic streaming, and semi-Definite Programming. Ultimately, with a storage of $k$ polynomial dimensions, our algorithm achieves a clustering solution of $(1\pm c_\Delta)$-approximation for any given $c_\Delta$ or $0 < c_\Delta < 1$, making it our current result for this problem. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to a plain Nash policy. Furthermore, the approach is adaptable to dynamic environments by prioritizing evasive agent's survival over maximizing rewards. We show that our method can be applied to a diverse range of grids, including those with obstacles, dynamic sizes, and changing terrain, and even scalable 3D worlds. The approach is also theoretically valuable as it facilitates an analytical examination of hierarchical structure's impact on survival probabilities. The code for the simulations is available online at https://github.com/akgupta93/hierarchical_pursuit_evasion. This perspective motivates an investigation of the accuracy of this "dressed" $W$-approximation, specifically in the context of high-energy muon collisions. To this end, a study is conducted to understand the limitations of this approximation, focusing on the energy range relevant to future muon colliders. A series of scattering processes off a $W$-boson are examined to assess the impact of this approximation on both its underlying physics and resulting experimental cross-section data. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based methods.
Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using a single shared dynamics model
to generate experiences for multiple tasks may actually decrease performance,
potentially causing a deterioration when tasks are highly distinct.
However, our key discovery reveals that using separate models for each task
greatly reduces 'catastrophic interference'--a phenomenon where the performance
on one task significantly drops after trying to solve another.
This effect becomes particularly pronounced under our proposed curriculum
learning strategy, which prioritizes difficult tasks.
As a result, our approach achieves superior performance in our experiments,
especially when tasks differ substantially.
Consequently, using separate models is essential for providing better
performance in our current multi-task reinforcement learning setup. 
This result has important implications for extending a small set of learned
skills to a large number of tasks. 
Our code can be found at https://github.com/ghulr/MixtureOfModels.

Additionally, we demonstrate how the model's confidence can be measured to guide the sampling process and determine optimal generation hyperparameters. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This finding is supported by other lines of evidence, including the duration of scintillation patterns and their orbital variations, and is also consistent with the limited extent of the void and the distant boundaries of the Local Bubble. This paper also explores various theoretical models for the formation and evolution of the Local Bubble, which could be related to the movement of the Sun through the galaxy or the collapse of the Local Bubble itself. The movement of the Sun through the galaxy results in the Sun's position changing over time, which in turn changes the orientation of the void and the screen's position relative to the line of sight to the pulsar, thereby affecting the duration of scintillation patterns and their orbital variations. In contrast, the collapse of the Local Bubble would lead to the disappearance of the screen and the void, along with other cavities in the Local Bubble, although this scenario is considered less plausible. The predicted times for the screen to disappear or the void to change significantly range from a few decades to a few centuries, which is consistent with the short duration of scintillation patterns observed in the data, and suggests that the timescale for the change in screen properties could be much faster than the timescale for the change in the void's dimensions. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given pitch cues by dynamically switching between pre-trained pitch-dependent convolutional neural networks. Secondly, the model includes an iterative signal decomposition module to enhance performance on non-stationary signals by leveraging its quasi-periodic characteristics. Experimental evaluations on both speech and medical signal generation demonstrate the superior performance of QPNet compared to WN and other baselines. The proposed framework also yields promising results for real-world applications, as it effectively generates signals outside the training frequency range with improved quality and mode-conditional control. The code for QPNet is available at https://github.com/ghru/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the model to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, without providing it any explicit instructions to do so. By training the model in this way, it develops an internal standard for difficult images, which it can then use to determine the location of sound sources within new, unseen images. Our experiments reveal that this method outperforms the current state-of-the-art model specifically in situations where the sound source and background are visually similar. Additionally, we propose a new problem called Unsupervised Sound Source Localization, where the model is trained on a single unlabeled video without any further training, and demonstrate that our approach can effectively solve this problem. Our code is available online at this link: https://github.com/ghamidi/VisSound.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using Lorentzian coordinates and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is demonstrated that this network achieves superior performance in comparison to standard hyperbolic GCNs on six datasets. Furthermore, LGCN's efficacy can be interpreted through the graph's topological characteristics, and it exhibits substantial advantages over current Hyperbolic GCNs when dealing with datasets featuring complex hierarchies. This network's code has been made publicly available at this https URL.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application is particularly well-suited
for problem-solving in fields like biomedicine, chemistry, and social sciences.
